strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: the paper correctly identifies that PIT-based recalibration only enforces a marginal (and hence weak) notion of calibration, while existing alternatives either quantify calibration error without correcting it (Moskvichev & Sejdinovic, 2025) or impose parametric assumptions (Song et al., 2019). The positioning against related work is thorough and fair.

The calibration–sharpness decomposition (Lemma 4.1) using generalized conditional mutual information induced by strictly proper scoring rules is elegant, and Appendix B shows it exactly matches the grouping loss of Kull & Flach (2015) and formalizes the Gneiting et al. (2007) calibration-sharpness conjecture (Prop. B.1). This is a genuinely useful conceptual contribution that clarifies why low CRPS/NLL does not imply reliability.

The proposed CKME-based recalibration (Algorithms 1-2) is a sensible nonparametric instantiation of the recalibration map Q -> P_{Y|Q}, removing the Gaussian-transformation assumption of Song et al. (2019) while inheriting consistency of conditional mean embeddings from Park & Muandet (2020).

The Energy Distance Kernel for real-valued targets, enabling O(n log n) kernel evaluation on empirical distributions, is a practical contribution that removes the quadratic bottleneck of generic distributional kernels; the ablation (Fig. 5) and wall-clock comparison (Fig. 7) support the efficiency claims.

The empirical protocol is comprehensive and reasonably rigorous: 4 base model classes x ~11 datasets x 20 pre-defined splits, evaluation via SKCE auto-calibration tests, KS-based PIT tests, relative CRPS, a comparison against split conformal prediction (Appendix D), and a comparison against kernelized distribution regression (Appendix F). Code is publicly available.

The paper demonstrates an important negative result (models improving overall score while remaining significantly miscalibrated) and includes an honest limitations section discussing computational cost, the weakness of auto-calibration relative to local/feature-conditional calibration, and the discarding of the density structure of the base model.
weaknesses: The abstract's claim that the method 'consistently outperforms prior re-calibration approaches' is not fully supported by the evidence. In Table 1, CKME yields the best relative CRPS in only a minority of settings; the no-recalibration baseline trained on train+calibration (None(T+C)) is frequently better, and CKME is sometimes substantially worse than the base model (e.g., GDN/yacht 1.276, MDN/housing 1.150). What is consistently demonstrated is better calibration test acceptance, which is a weaker claim than the one stated.

The headline theoretical property (auto-calibration of the recalibrated prediction, Prop. 5.2) holds for the oracle recalibrated prediction, but the implemented pipeline introduces approximations with no formal guarantees: the Euclidean projection of the CKME weights onto the simplex (Eq. 40) instead of the proper pre-image problem (Eq. 39) is acknowledged as an implementation choice, and no finite-sample error bound or consistency result is given for the final pipeline. The paper thus does not prove that the output of Algorithm 2 is auto-calibrated, even asymptotically; the evidence is empirical test non-rejection only.

Evidence of calibration rests on accepting the null hypothesis of SKCE tests at alpha = 5%. Non-rejection is weak evidence, particularly on small test sets (yacht: 31, housing: 51) where power is low; the authors annotate test sizes and are aware of this, but no power analysis is performed, and multiple-testing across ~800 dataset/model/split combinations is not addressed.

The algorithmic novelty is moderate: the CKME estimator and KRR-style coefficients are standard (Song et al., 2009; Park & Muandet, 2020; Christmann & Steinwart, 2010), and the O(n log n) evaluation follows from the known equivalence between energy distance and RKHS distances (Sejdinovic et al., 2013). The main theoretical results (Lemma 4.1, Props. A.2-A.3) largely restate or adapt known decompositions (Brocker 2009; Kull & Flach 2015; Dawid & Musio 2014), with Prop. A.4 and B.1 being the main new but straightforward additions.

The recalibrated prediction is an empirical distribution supported only on the calibration-set targets (plus the Euclidean-projection approximation), which changes the character of the output (e.g., piecewise-constant CDF); the paper acknowledges this discards the density structure of the base model, but the practical consequences for downstream tasks requiring densities or fine-grained quantiles are not evaluated.

Several presentation issues reduce clarity: the bar-chart summaries in Figures 1-3 are difficult to read and interpret quantitatively; the discussion of sharpness is indirect (sharpening cannot be assessed directly); and the wall-clock comparison in Figure 7 depends heavily on the authors' PIT implementation choice (sampling 1000 points for density models), which may overstate the efficiency advantage.

Some experimental details are under-specified in the main text, e.g., sensitivity to the kernel bandwidth and regularization hyperparameters is handled via median heuristics and 5-fold CV on the calibration set, but no sensitivity analysis is reported, despite these being known to strongly affect kernel calibration estimates.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and well-motivated gap: post-hoc recalibration of regression models under the strong notion of auto-calibration, without the parametric assumptions of Song et al. (2019) or the weakness of marginal PIT calibration. The positioning against PIT recalibration (Kuleshov et al., 2018), GPBETA, and conformal prediction is clearly argued.

The calibration–sharpness decomposition (Lemma 4.1) using generalized conditional mutual information is clean and pedagogically valuable, and Appendix B nicely connects it to the grouping loss of Kull & Flach (2015) and gives a formal statement of the Gneiting et al. (2007) sharpness-subject-to-calibration paradigm (Proposition B.1).

The Energy Distance Kernel is a practical contribution: instantiating the Gaussian-type kernel of Christmann & Steinwart (2010) with the energy distance yields an O(m log m) evaluation for empirical distributions, removing a quadratic bottleneck, with an ablation study (Appendix E) and wall-clock comparison (Appendix G) supporting the efficiency claim.

The experimental protocol is broad: 4 base model families (GDN, MDN, BNN, DRF), 11 datasets, 20 predefined splits, comparison against both recalibrated and non-recalibrated baselines (None(T) vs None(T+C)), plus appendices comparing to conformal prediction and to direct kernelized distribution regression. Code is publicly released.

The limitations section is honest and substantive: it correctly identifies the O(n_cal^3) cost, the weakness relative to feature-conditional (local) calibration, and the fact that the method outputs an empirical distribution and discards density structure.
weaknesses: A gap between theoretical guarantees and the actual algorithm. Proposition 5.2 shows the idealized recalibrated prediction Q̃ = P_{Y|Q} is auto-calibrated in the population, but the implemented estimator involves (i) CKME regression, (ii) an ad hoc Euclidean projection of β onto the simplex instead of solving the actual pre-image problem (Eq. 39 vs 40), and (iii) support restriction to calibration-set targets. No finite-sample calibration guarantee is given for the output of Algorithm 2, yet the abstract claims the algorithm is 'capable of correcting calibration error.'

The headline empirical evidence is statistically weak in framing: the main calibration result (Figure 1) reports the fraction of splits in which the SKCE test *failed to reject* the null of auto-calibration. Acceptance of a null hypothesis is not evidence of calibration, particularly on very small test sets (yacht has 31 test points), where power is low. The paper acknowledges this only implicitly via test-set sizes; a more convincing evaluation would report effect sizes or consistent SKCE values rather than acceptance rates.

Potential evaluation circularity: the SKCE test used to evaluate the method employs the Energy Distance Kernel, i.e., the same kernel family used to train the recalibration. This risks optimizing toward the evaluation metric, and no alternative calibration metric is used to check the auto-calibration claim.

The claim of 'consistently outperforming prior re-calibration approaches' is not supported by Table 1. CRPS improvements over the unmodified base model are typically marginal (<5%), the simple baseline None(T+C) frequently matches or beats CKME, and on several datasets CKME causes large regressions (e.g., yacht: 1.276 for GDN, 1.326 for MDN, 1.614 for BNN — up to 61% worse CRPS). The abstract's consistency claim should be substantially tempered.

Modest technical novelty beyond combination of known components: conditional kernel mean embeddings (Song et al., 2009; Park & Muandet, 2020), Gaussian-type distributional kernels (Christmann & Steinwart, 2010), energy-distance computations (Székely & Rizzo; Baringhaus & Franz 2004; Bodenham & Kawahara 2023), and the recalibration proposition (Brocker 2009; Widmann 2021) are all existing. The decomposition largely recovers Kull & Flach (2015) and Gruber & Buettner (2024). The paper is candid about this, but the contribution is incremental.

Practical deployability concerns are underexplored: the output is a discrete empirical distribution over calibration targets, which is awkward for continuous targets and downstream use; performance degrades sharply on small calibration sets (n_cal ≈ 30–50 for several datasets); and PIT recalibration remains superior on the paper's own weaker-calibration metric (Figure 3), meaning the method trades PIT performance for a stronger notion whose empirical verification rests on the weak acceptance-rate analysis above.

Presentation issues: multiple broken references ('Our experiment code is publicly available at' followed by blank; Appendix D and F source-code URLs empty), a typo in footnote 1 ('I(I; X)'), and Figures 1/3 as acceptance-fraction bar charts are difficult to interpret quantitatively.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and well-motivated gap: post-hoc recalibration for regression under a strong notion of calibration (auto-calibration), avoiding both the weakness of PIT-based recalibration (error cancellation) and the restrictive parametric assumptions of Song et al. (2019). This positioning is clearly argued and well grounded in the calibration literature (Gneiting & Resin, Tsyplakov, Widmann et al.).

The theoretical framing is solid and adds understanding. Lemma 4.1 gives a clean calibration–sharpness–aleatoric decomposition of the expected score using generalized conditional mutual information, and Appendix B formally connects this to the grouping loss of Kull & Flach (2015) and formalizes the Gneiting et al. (2007) 'sharpness subject to calibration' paradigm (Prop. B.1), which was previously only conjectural. Proposition 5.2 correctly shows the ideal recalibrated prediction is auto-calibrated and sharpness-preserving.

The evaluation is unusually thorough for this problem area: 11 datasets (UCI benchmark plus bike sharing and a synthetic bimodal set), 4 heterogeneous base models (GDN, MDN, BNN, DRF), 20 repeated splits, two hypothesis-test-based calibration evaluations (SKCE and KS-based PIT) plus CRPS, and additional appendices comparing against conformal prediction, kernelized distribution regression, wall-clock timing, and kernel efficiency ablations. Evaluation via a consistent hypothesis test rather than a point metric is the right methodology for calibration claims.

Reproducibility is good: implementation details are extensive (bandwidth heuristics, cross-validated regularization, GPBETA Gaussian-approximation caveat), and experiment code is stated to be publicly available, with baseline implementations from the original authors where possible.

The limitations section is honest and substantive, correctly identifying the O(n^3_cal) linear-system cost, that the output is an empirical distribution that discards density structure, and that auto-calibration is weaker than feature-conditional (local) calibration.
weaknesses: The abstract's central claim that the method 'consistently outperforms prior re-calibration approaches' is not supported by the evidence. Table 1 shows CKME is frequently worse than both baselines and even the un-recalibrated model on CRPS (e.g., GDN yacht 1.276, MDN yacht 1.326, BNN yacht 1.614, housing entries ~1.15), and the simply retrained None(T+C) baseline is competitive or better on many rows. The superiority claim holds mainly for SKCE test acceptance, which is a noisier and less interpretable criterion.

The hypothesis-test-based evidence has a power problem that the paper acknowledges only implicitly. Acceptance of auto-calibration at α=5% on small test sets (31–51 observations) provides weak evidence of calibration; on the larger datasets the method performs better, but the aggregated Figure 1 presentation conflates datasets where acceptance may reflect low power rather than good calibration. A power analysis or size-controlled comparison would strengthen the conclusion considerably.

Novelty is somewhat overstated. The recalibration algorithm is a direct assembly of existing components: Gaussian-type kernels over distributions (Christmann & Steinwart 2010), conditional kernel mean embeddings (Song et al. 2009; Park & Muandet 2020), and the O(n log n) evaluation of energy-distance-type kernels on R (which the paper itself cites as known in Section 3.2.1, e.g., Baringhaus & Franz 2004; Bodenham & Kawahara 2023). The EDK is essentially the known energy-distance instantiation of the Gaussian-type kernel; this should be framed more modestly.

The end-to-end pipeline lacks theoretical guarantees. Consistency is cited only for the raw CKME estimator; the heuristic pre-image step (Euclidean projection of β onto the simplex, replacing the correct quadratic-regularized problem (39) with (40)) and the empirical-support restriction mean the deployed estimator Q̃ is not shown to converge to the auto-calibrated target, and the approximation error is not quantified.

Only one recalibration baseline from the PIT family is evaluated head-to-head, and GPBETA requires Gaussian approximation of the base model output, which disadvantages it against distributional baselines. The comparison with Marx et al. (2023) is discussed but not tested. Given the mixed CRPS results, stronger baseline coverage would be needed to support the 'state-of-the-art' framing in the conclusions.

Some presentation issues: the code repository URLs in Section 6 and Appendices D/F are left blank ('available at .'), and Figure 5 reports an unexplained performance spike that is attributed speculatively to GPU parallelization without resolution.
